strengths: Originality: Applying discrete graph diffusion to directional ad hoc topology generation is a relevant combination, and the proposed cross-attentive modulation (CAM) token offers a plausible lightweight mechanism for injecting graph-level information into node and edge representations.

Soundness: The paper evaluates several practically relevant properties, including connectivity, parity, range, throughput, and antenna-sector saturation. The ablations indicate that the specialized losses materially improve their corresponding constraints: saturated antennas decrease from 23.38% to 16.19%, while parity adherence rises from 67.07% to 98.65%.

Significance: Fast topology construction under node movement could be useful for software-defined directional wireless networks, and learning from expensive optimization outputs is a sensible problem formulation.
Presentation: The high-level motivation, denoising pipeline, CAM mechanism, and post-processing procedure are reasonably easy to follow, with helpful architecture and diffusion illustrations.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central operational claims are not adequately supported. Although network evolution under moving nodes is presented as a main contribution, there are no mobility experiments, trajectory protocols, topology-stability measurements, reconfiguration counts, temporal throughput results, or comparisons against recomputation. The assertion that a previous topology is effectively analogous to a noisy training graph is not theoretically or empirically established.

Soundness: The generated graphs remain substantially inferior to the targets on important physical properties: they have 49.74 rather than 43.90 links, average link length 1.04 rather than 0.85, throughput 1.60 rather than 1.72, and 16.19% rather than 9.74% saturated antennas. Moreover, 12.31% of nodes are saturated and 0.87% of graphs are disconnected. These are material violations for a system described as operational, yet results after the corrective algorithm are not reported.

Evaluation and significance: The only substantive learned baseline is a standard graph-transformer DDPM. There is no comparison with the greedy teacher on end-to-end runtime and quality, simpler supervised edge predictors, constructive heuristics, optimization methods, or other graph generators. Thus the evidence does not establish that diffusion or CAM is necessary, nor that the proposed system actually alleviates the computational burden relative to practical alternatives.

Originality: CAM closely resembles established global/register-token attention combined with FiLM-style modulation. The paper does not compare against global pooling, virtual nodes, ordinary graph tokens, registers, or parameter-matched alternatives, so its distinct contribution and the cause of the reported gains remain unclear. The ablation also conflates CAM with other architectural differences.

Reproducibility: Essential information is missing, including exact dataset sizes and splits, node-position and rotation distributions, the complete teacher algorithm and heuristic, interference and range parameters, network simulator details, loss weights, model dimensions, batch size, epochs, optimizer settings beyond a very broad learning-rate interval, checkpoint selection, random seeds, and sampling details. No code or dataset availability statement is provided.

Statistical reliability: The manuscript describes the test set only as “thousands” of random 16-node instances and reports single aggregate values without sample counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or multi-seed results. The claimed 32-node generalization is explicitly anecdotal and unsupported by a proper test set.

Technical clarity: Several definitions are inconsistent or incomplete. Equation 4 omits the softmax from standard cross-attention despite Figure 2 including it; the diffusion posterior and transition scalar are underspecified; loss normalization and weighting are absent; and the parity metric is described as the proportion of violating links even though higher values are treated as better. “Saturated nodes” and “saturated antennas” measure different phenomena but are used somewhat interchangeably.

Scalability is not convincingly demonstrated. Experiments are restricted to 16 nodes, the 32-node result is qualitative, and the reported 480 ms diffusion plus up to 250 ms post-processing is not compared fairly with the teacher or other algorithms. Algorithm 2 also lacks a failure or termination condition when disconnected components cannot be joined through mutually compatible free sectors.

Presentation and limitations: The prose contains numerous typographical and grammatical errors, and important physical-model details are deferred rather than explained. The limitations discussion mentions the missing 32-node dataset and unstudied step skipping, but omits the more consequential constraint-violation rates, distribution shift, feasibility failures, and dependence on centralized state.

Ethics and deployment: No acute ethical issue is evident, but a networking system that can output disconnected or physically invalid topologies warrants discussion of fail-safe validation, robustness under localization errors or distribution shift, and the consequences of deployment failures. The post-processing check is described informally rather than validated as a reliable safety mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: rapidly constructing directional ad hoc-network topologies under geometric and connectivity constraints. Conditioning graph generation on node locations is a sensible formulation.

The combination of discrete edge diffusion, constraint-aware features and losses, and CAM-token modulation is coherent. The ablations provide preliminary evidence that the added losses reduce saturated antennas from 23.38% to 16.19% and substantially improve parity compliance, while the full model improves over the standard graph transformer on several reported metrics.

The manuscript is organized clearly, and its figures and tables are readable. It also acknowledges some limitations, including excess generated links, reliance on post-processing, and the lack of a full 32-node dataset. weaknesses: Soundness: the evidence does not support several central claims. The proposed network-evolution method is not evaluated at all, despite being presented as robust and efficient. There are no mobility experiments measuring topology churn, constraint violations, throughput over time, or comparison with recomputation and temporal baselines.

Soundness: the evaluation omits the stated central interference objective. It reports connectivity, parity, distance, and a briefly described throughput measure, but no interference, scheduling, latency, routing, robustness, or end-to-end operational metric. Generated graphs also differ materially from the targets: 49.74 versus 43.90 links, average length 1.04 versus 0.85, and 16.19% versus 9.74% saturated antennas.

Soundness and significance: comparisons are limited to a standard graph-transformer DDPM and partial ablations. There is no comparison with the teacher greedy algorithm on runtime and solution quality, simple geometric heuristics, combinatorial approximations, other graph generators, or the closely related wireless graph-diffusion work cited as reference 18. Thus neither the claimed computational advantage nor the usefulness of diffusion is established.

The claimed operational guarantee depends on an unevaluated post-processing algorithm. Its component-connection loop is not shown to terminate when compatible free antenna sectors do not exist, and the paper does not report final metrics after correction. Consequently, the claim that outputs require only minor corrections and are operational is unsupported.

The scalability claim is weak: experiments focus on only 16 nodes, while the 32-node result is described merely as having “seemed” similar without a dataset or quantitative results. Reporting 480 ms GPU and 2 s CPU inference is not informative without batch size, variance, post-processing cost, or a runtime comparison against the greedy teacher and other baselines.

The mathematical specification contains consequential ambiguities and inconsistencies. The purported standard cross-attention equation omits softmax; the binary transition “matrix” is described as a scalar; the reverse posterior and sampling equations are not fully defined; notation alternates between node-level parity and indexed parity quantities; and it is unclear whether nondifferentiable graph statistics in the auxiliary losses are computed from hard edges or probabilities.

Presentation suffers from unclear metric definitions. For example, “Parity” is described as the proportion of links that do not respect parity, yet higher is marked better and 98.65% is interpreted as strong compliance. The manuscript also lacks uncertainty estimates, significance tests, exact sample counts, and per-instance distributions, so the small differences in Table 1 cannot be judged reliably.

Originality appears incremental. Global/register tokens, cross-attention, FiLM-style modulation, discrete graph diffusion, guided sampling, and constraint penalties are established ingredients. CAM may be a useful combination, but the experiments do not cleanly isolate its effect or compare it with simpler global-token, virtual-node, or graph-statistic conditioning alternatives.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper provides neither code nor data and deliberately leaves the teacher topology algorithm unspecified. It omits dataset size and generation distribution, train/validation/test splits, physical and interference thresholds, throughput-simulator details, architectural dimensions, number of heads and tokens, loss weights, exact learning rate, epochs, batch size, seeds, and complete diffusion/post-processing settings.

Limitations and ethics are treated insufficiently. There is no dedicated limitations or broader-impact discussion covering distribution shift, failure detection, adversarial or faulty nodes, reliability consequences of invalid deployed topologies, or the dual-use implications of automated wireless-network design. These concerns are especially relevant because the paper repeatedly characterizes the system as operational.

Overall, the work has a discernible idea and encouraging preliminary numbers, so a strong reject is unwarranted. However, missing evaluation of mobility and interference, inadequate baselines, under-specified methods, and poor reproducibility prevent the central claims from being trusted or built upon; these are substantial issues requiring a new experimental study rather than minor revision.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically meaningful problem: rapidly constructing directional ad hoc network topologies subject to connectivity, parity, range, and antenna-sector constraints.

Conditioning discrete graph diffusion on fixed node geometry is a sensible formulation, and the proposed CAM mechanism provides a plausible lightweight way to inject graph-level information into node and edge processing.

The component ablations are directionally useful. Compared with the standard graph transformer, NetDiff improves connectedness (98.12% to 99.13%) and reduces saturated nodes (17.08% to 12.31%); the specialized losses substantially improve saturated-antenna and parity metrics.
The paper connects generation to deployment through a concrete post-processing algorithm and reports inference and correction latency, rather than evaluating graph similarity alone.
The manuscript is generally readable, motivates the application well, and includes an architecture diagram and explicit constraint metrics.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is too limited to support the central operational and scalability claims. Experiments mainly concern random 16-node instances, while the 32-node result is only described informally as having “seemed” similar. There are no systematic scaling curves, stress tests, statistical uncertainty, or evaluation under diverse spatial distributions.

The proposed network-evolution method is a major claimed contribution but receives no quantitative evaluation. The paper does not measure topology churn, constraint violations, throughput, latency, or robustness as nodes move, so the claimed stable and robust temporal behavior is unsupported.

Baselines are inadequate. Evaluation only contrasts architectural variants of essentially the same diffusion approach; it does not compare topology quality and end-to-end runtime against the greedy data-generating algorithm, other heuristic/optimization methods, or relevant learned graph-generation approaches.

Reproducibility is poor: the manuscript omits dataset sizes and splits, node-position and rotation distributions, physical/interference-model parameters, loss weights, embedding dimensions, attention heads, training duration, diffusion details, random seeds, and exact evaluation sample counts. No code or data availability statement is provided.

Several methodological definitions are incomplete or questionable. The displayed cross-attention equation omits softmax; the discrete transition process and scalar data-aware matrix are insufficiently specified; the differentiable implementation of topology-dependent losses is unclear; and guided sampling is introduced without enough detail to reproduce it.

Reported results remain materially short of the target topologies: NetDiff produces 49.74 versus 43.90 links, average link length 1.04 versus 0.85, throughput 1.60 versus 1.72, and 16.19% versus 9.74% saturated antennas. The claim that only minor corrections are needed is not backed by post-correction quality statistics or correction-frequency measurements.

The evaluation does not directly report interference, despite interference reduction being a principal motivation. Throughput simulation is also under-specified, preventing assessment of whether it faithfully represents the intended wireless setting.

The complexity argument overlooks the cost of 50 denoising passes and is not supported by runtime comparisons across graph sizes. A reported 480 ms GPU generation time plus up to 250 ms of correction does not by itself establish superiority over the original heuristic.

Originality is moderate rather than strong: CAM appears closely related to global/register tokens combined with cross-attention and FiLM-style modulation. The paper does not sharply distinguish its mechanism theoretically or empirically from these existing designs.

Presentation contains numerous typographical and definitional issues, including inconsistent descriptions of the parity metric and saturation constraints. There is also no dedicated limitations or research-ethics discussion; relevant deployment risks such as failures under distribution shift and reliance on corrective safety checks are not addressed.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important combinatorial problem: rapidly constructing directional mobile-network topologies under connectivity, sector, interference, and half-duplex constraints.

The proposed ACAM mechanism is intuitive: unnormalized cross-attention aggregates graph-level cardinality information, while FiLM communicates it back to node and edge representations. The method is described reasonably clearly with equations and a diagram.

The experiments contain useful component-level evidence. Relative to CAM, ACAM improves link throughput from 3.40 to 3.52 and saturation from 12.9% to 12.1% in Table 1; Table 3 likewise reports lower node saturation (7.05% versus 7.98%). The specialized losses also substantially improve parity compliance in Table 4.
Partial diffusion is a potentially useful approach to topology reconfiguration, and the reported 3.3–5x sampling speedup is promising.

The appendix provides pseudocode for the fallback heuristic and topology correction routine, and the impact statement appropriately recognizes deployment and misuse risks. The manuscript is generally readable and visually well organized. weaknesses: Soundness: the central performance evidence depends on an incompletely specified proprietary simulator and training-data generator. The paper omits antenna patterns, propagation and attenuation parameters, search budget, fallback frequency, dataset size and construction statistics, train/validation/test splits, and test sample counts. Consequently, neither the targets nor the claimed throughput can be independently validated.

Soundness: the strongest result in Table 2 is not an isolated evaluation of the learned model. The text says that all results except throughput are obtained without post-processing, implying that throughput uses the optimization-based correction routine. That routine explicitly adds edges by maximizing throughput and prunes harmful edges, yet its contribution is not ablated and its runtime is only asserted to be below 100 ms. Raw-model throughput, correction gains, failure rates, and corrected baseline results are missing.

Soundness: comparisons are insufficiently controlled and sometimes internally inconsistent. The manuscript says all models use the additional features and losses, while Table 1 separately lists “DDPM-GT” and “DDPM-GT w/ features.” Architecture sizes, tuning budgets, parameter counts, training costs, and post-processing parity across baselines are not reported. Comparisons mainly involve weak VAE models and a locally defined DDPM-GT rather than strong contemporary combinatorial solvers or the closely related TopoFormer.

Soundness: uncertainty reporting is not interpretable. Values such as ±0.05 are given without stating whether they are standard deviations, standard errors, confidence intervals, or variation across samples/seeds. Only one training seed is specified, early stopping uses unspecified “crucial performance metrics,” and no hypothesis tests or multi-seed results are supplied.

The partial-diffusion claims are weakly supported. There is no comparison against warm-started optimization, direct prediction, graph-editing, or reuse-and-repair baselines; “continuity,” normalized displacement, realistic trajectories, and the accuracy–computation tradeoff are not rigorously defined. Tables 5–6 also provide no full-diffusion control under the same perturbed layouts.

Originality is moderate rather than compellingly established. ACAM is essentially an unnormalized global attention/sum-aggregation token followed by FiLM, closely related to virtual-node, global pooling, and DeepSets-style mechanisms. The paper provides neither a formal expressivity result nor broad experiments demonstrating an advantage beyond this single proprietary task.

Significance and generalization are limited by evaluation on a narrow setting, primarily 16-node layouts. The 32-node model must be retrained on 32-node examples and remains noticeably behind the target; networks above 40 nodes are excluded. Claims of size-agnostic behavior and “constant inference time” are therefore overstated, since dense edge prediction scales with graph size and correction has data-dependent runtime.

Presentation and specification leave important technical ambiguities: loss weights are absent; the number of ACAM tokens and pooling rule are not fixed in the main configuration; several sampling equations are underspecified; the cosine loss is potentially undefined for nodes with fewer than two neighbors; and “saturation” changes between antenna-level and node-level tables without a precise unified definition.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the main-track standard. No code, data, complete simulator, preprocessing procedure, checkpoint-selection rule, or exhaustive hyperparameter specification is provided, and the proprietary physical parameters are precisely those needed to reproduce the headline throughput result. The ethics discussion is reasonable, but it does not remedy this evidential limitation.

strengths: The method targets a concrete constrained optimization problem where fast inference could be practically valuable. Joint prediction of links and transmit/receive parity is well motivated.

ACAM is a plausible lightweight global-conditioning mechanism: unnormalized cross-attention can retain cardinality information, and the CAM-to-ACAM ablation reports consistent improvements in saturation and throughput-related statistics.
The paper evaluates several model families, provides a 32-node experiment, and includes pseudocode for the heuristic fallback and topology correction.
The manuscript is generally readable and visually organized. Its impact statement acknowledges dual-use and deployment-validation risks without obvious unresolved ethical violations.
weaknesses: Soundness is not established because the central supervision and evaluation oracle is insufficiently specified. The simulation-guided quasi-exhaustive search is not described algorithmically, while exact simulator parameters are omitted due to proprietary antenna patterns, propagation models, attenuation laws, and an external power-control module. Neither target quality nor reported throughput can therefore be independently reproduced or audited.

The strongest throughput evidence is confounded by post-processing. The paper states that every result except throughput is measured without post-processing, while Algorithm 2 uses the same throughput/interference model to add and remove links, maximize throughput gain, repair connectivity, and prune edges. It is unclear whether every baseline receives identical correction, and raw-throughput, correction-only, and correction-cost ablations are absent. Table 2 therefore cannot attribute its gains to NetDiff.

Experimental reporting is inadequate: the main dataset sizes and splits, number of evaluated graphs and samples, seed aggregation, early-stopping criterion, loss weights, parameter counts, and baseline-tuning budgets are absent. Only one training seed is given, while the meaning of the reported plus/minus values is undefined.

Several technical definitions are ambiguous or potentially incorrect. Equation 4 does not clearly give the normalized posterior marginalization required for discrete diffusion; Equations 5-6 combine objects with unclear dimensions; guided discrete sampling is underspecified; Equation 15 has unclear indexing and can be undefined for nodes with fewer than two neighbors; Equation 16 does not explain differentiability through predicted parity; and the edge-angle feature uses arctan rather than atan2.

Claims about constraint satisfaction and real-time operation are overstated. Raw outputs retain nonzero disconnection, parity-violation, and sector-saturation rates, while the correction loop may explicitly terminate while disconnected. Its claimed sub-100-ms runtime lacks a distributional benchmark and is solution-dependent, undermining the broad claim of constant inference time. Full generation itself takes about 450 ms on a T4 and up to 2 seconds on CPU.

The mobility evaluation is too weak to support the network-evolution contribution. Realistic trajectories, displacement normalization, continuity, and the mapping from displacement to diffusion time are not adequately defined. There is no tabulated full-diffusion comparison, dynamic heuristic, solver reference on moved layouts, multi-step rollout, or realistic simulator evaluation. Greater similarity to an old topology is not inherently beneficial and could indicate failure to adapt.

Originality is weakened by missing comparisons to straightforward alternatives. ACAM resembles unnormalized global aggregation followed by FiLM, but it is not compared with sum pooling, virtual nodes, Set-Transformer-style pooling, or explicitly supplied global counts. The incremental gain over CAM is modest, lacks significance testing, and additional favorable experiments are omitted.

The evaluation is narrow and internally inconsistent. It is almost entirely synthetic and centered on 16-node graphs. The 32-node model is trained on 32-node examples, so size generalization is not demonstrated, and larger cases are excluded. Saturation values differ substantially between Tables 1 and 3 without a clear metric distinction, and the statement that all models use extra features conflicts with the separate DDPM-GT-with-features row. Overall, the manuscript contains a promising idea, but the proprietary oracle, confounded evaluation, and incomplete mathematical and reproducibility details are acceptance-blocking.

strengths: Originality/significance: NetDiff addresses a practically meaningful constrained graph-generation problem and jointly predicts topology and transmit/receive parity. The proposed ACAM mechanism—unsoftmaxed cross-attention aggregation followed by FiLM modulation—is a simple, potentially reusable way to expose graph transformers to permutation-invariant global count information.

Soundness: The component ablations are directionally convincing. Relative to DDPM-GT, CAM/ACAM improves antenna saturation from 11.62% to 7.98%/7.05% while maintaining approximately 98.7% connectivity and parity compliance. The loss ablation also shows that the added constraint losses materially improve saturation and parity.

The reported throughput results are promising: NetDiff nearly matches the target on 16-node instances (78.92 versus 79.33 Mbps) and improves substantially over DDPM-GT on the reported 32-node setting (322.40 versus 258.90 Mbps).

Partial diffusion is a useful extension for mobile networks: the paper reports comparable constraint satisfaction with 10–15 steps, 3.3–5x faster inference, and greater continuity with the previous topology.

Presentation: The problem motivation is clear, the architecture is illustrated effectively, and the appendix supplies pseudocode for the fallback solver and correction procedure. The impact statement acknowledges deployment and misuse risks appropriately.
weaknesses: Soundness: The empirical evidence is too limited to support the broad claims. Evaluation uses a single private simulation setting, primarily unseen 16-node graphs, with only a small additional 32-node study. There are no results across deployment distributions, mobility regimes, antenna/channel models, or substantially different graph sizes.

The paper omits essential experimental details: dataset size and splits, number of test instances and independent runs, training compute, early-stopping rule, loss weights, ACAM-token count used in main results, perturbation distributions, and many simulator parameters. Consequently, the meaning of the reported ± values and whether improvements are statistically reliable are unclear.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The appendix explicitly omits exact propagation, attenuation, antenna-pattern, and simulation parameters because they are proprietary, and no code or data-release statement is given. These parameters define both supervision and the principal throughput metric, so others cannot reconstruct the central evaluation.

The target labels mix quasi-exhaustive optimization with an underspecified heuristic fallback, without reporting fallback frequency, solver budget, or optimality gaps. Thus, target quality is unknown, and matching this target does not establish closeness to an optimum.

Baseline coverage is insufficient. TopoFormer is identified as closely related but not evaluated; there are no modern combinatorial-learning or optimization baselines, and the VAE comparisons are weak. It is also unclear whether all baselines received equivalent tuning and domain-specific losses/features.

Several headline claims overreach the measurements. Throughput is only a theoretical instantaneous upper-bound proxy excluding routing and scheduling, not realized end-to-end network performance. The claim of constant inference time holds only for a fixed number of denoising steps and ignores graph-transformer scaling with node count. The assertion that ACAM captures long-range interference is not directly tested.

The partial-diffusion study lacks strong controls, such as warm-started optimization, direct prediction from the moved layout, or alternative temporal models. Its trajectory generation, continuity definition, displacement normalization, and accuracy–computation trade-off are not specified precisely enough to validate the mobility claims.

Presentation has technical ambiguities: the reverse-sampling equations do not fully specify normalized transition probabilities, the transition-matrix notation involving a one-dimensional marginal is unclear, and the cosine loss indexing is difficult to reconcile with its stated purpose. The post-processing discussion also leaves ambiguity about which reported metrics use correction.

The 32-node evidence is especially hard to interpret: it comes from a separately retrained mixed-size model trained for only an 'equivalent of 2 epochs,' while uncertainty and matched architectural baselines are absent. Moreover, performance remains noticeably behind the target on link count and saturation, and networks above 40 nodes are excluded.

Ethics/limitations: The impact statement is adequate, but operational safety needs more concrete treatment because the correction algorithm can explicitly terminate while leaving the network disconnected. There is no robustness or failure-case analysis for deployment under distribution shift. Overall, the idea is promising, but these evidential and reproducibility gaps currently prevent others from reliably validating or building on the contribution.
